Summer can affect mental health in different ways. For some people, sunshine and longer days may improve mood. For others, rising temperatures can worsen anxiety, low mood, irritability, fatigue, and poor sleep.

Heat places extra stress on the body, can disturb sleep, and may intensify physical sensations like a racing heart or restlessness, which can feel similar to anxiety. Poor sleep during warmer nights can also affect concentration, emotional balance, and energy levels.

At the same time, simple protective habits can make a real difference: staying hydrated, keeping a regular routine, gentle movement, rest, and spending time in calming natural spaces.

In simple terms: summer can boost mood when the body is well-regulated. Prioritising sleep, hydration, and rest is not just self-care~it is mental health care.

🧠 ADHD: Myths vs Facts

ADHD is one of the most misunderstood neurodevelopmental conditions. Unfortunately, myths and misconceptions can delay diagnosis, increase stigma, and prevent individuals from getting the support they need.

❌ Myth: ADHD is caused by poor parenting.
✅ Fact: ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition with strong genetic and biological influences.

❌ Myth: Only hyperactive children have ADHD.
✅ Fact: Many individuals, especially girls, may primarily struggle with inattention and organization.

❌ Myth: Children outgrow ADHD.
✅ Fact: While symptoms may change over time, ADHD often continues into adolescence and adulthood.

❌ Myth: ADHD means low intelligence.
✅ Fact: People with ADHD can be highly intelligent, creative, innovative, and successful.

Understanding the facts helps us move away from judgment and toward support, early intervention, and effective treatment.

Have you heard any of these myths before? Let us know in the comments. 👇

🚨 Common Signs of ADHD in Children 🚨

ADHD is more than just being energetic or easily distracted. It is a neurodevelopmental condition that can affect attention, behavior, emotional regulation, and daily functioning.

Some common signs include:
✔️ Difficulty paying attention
✔️ Excessive fidgeting or restlessness
✔️ Acting without thinking
✔️ Trouble following instructions
✔️ Frequent forgetfulness
✔️ Disorganization
✔️ Easily distracted by surroundings
✔️ Emotional outbursts or frustration

Every child may show some of these behaviors occasionally. However, when these difficulties are persistent, occur across different settings (home and school), and interfere with daily life, a professional evaluation may be helpful.

Early identification and support can make a significant difference in a child’s academic, social, and emotional development.

If you have concerns about your child’s attention, behavior, or learning, consult a best psychiatrist in Borivali east for guidance. Our doctor is best psychiatrist near Borivali east.

What is ADHD?

ADHD (Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder) is a neurodevelopmental condition that affects attention, impulse control, and activity levels. It can impact academic performance, work, relationships, and daily functioning, but with proper understanding and support, individuals with ADHD can thrive.

🔹 Inattentive Type
Often appears as distractibility, forgetfulness, difficulty staying organized, and trouble sustaining attention. These individuals may seem quiet, daydreamy, or “lost in thought.”

🔹 Hyperactive-Impulsive Type
Characterized by excessive movement, restlessness, impulsive decisions, frequent interruptions, and difficulty waiting one’s turn.

🔹 Combined Type
The most common presentation, involving symptoms of both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity.

Independence is often seen as a sign of strength. However, for some people, being highly self-sufficient can make it difficult to recognise when support is needed or to feel comfortable asking for it.

Over time, constantly managing everything alone can contribute to stress, emotional exhaustion, and isolation.
True emotional wellbeing includes knowing when to rely on your own strengths and when to allow others to support you.

We've shared a thoughtful reflection on this in our latest blog. You can read it anytime on our website.

The Problem With Always Being the Reliable One: Being dependable is often seen as a strength, and it is. Many people take pride in being the person others can count on during difficult times.

However, constantly being the one who carries responsibility, offers support, and keeps things together can sometimes come at a personal cost. Over time, it may become difficult to acknowledge your own needs, ask for help, or allow yourself to rest.
Emotional wellbeing includes recognising that strength and vulnerability can coexist. Even the most reliable people deserve support, understanding, and care.

We’ve shared a thoughtful reflection on this in our latest blog. You can read it anytime on our website.

The Relief of Realising You Don’t Need to Be Good at Everything:
Many people place significant pressure on themselves to perform well across every area of life. While striving for growth can be valuable, constantly expecting perfection can lead to stress, self-criticism, and exhaustion.

Learning to accept limitations, embrace learning, and focus on what truly matters can create a healthier and more sustainable relationship with personal growth.
Self-worth is not determined by being exceptional at everything. Sometimes, wellbeing begins with allowing yourself to be human.

We’ve shared a thoughtful reflection on this in our latest blog. You can read it anytime on our website.

Uncertainty can feel uncomfortable, especially when we are searching for clarity about decisions, relationships, or the future. It's natural to want answers quickly.

However, not all clarity arrives through immediate problem-solving. Some understanding develops through time, experience, and allowing situations to unfold.
Learning to tolerate uncertainty can reduce stress, ease overthinking, and create space for greater trust in the process of life.

We’ve shared a thoughtful reflection on this in our latest blog. You can read it anytime on our website.

Many people carry emotional responsibilities that were never fully theirs to hold. This can include feeling responsible for other people's moods, reactions, decisions, or disappointments.

While empathy and care are important, constantly taking on what belongs to others can lead to stress, guilt, and emotional exhaustion. Learning to distinguish between supporting others and carrying their burdens can create healthier relationships, clearer boundaries, and greater emotional wellbeing.

We’ve shared a thoughtful reflection on this in our latest blog. You can read it anytime on our website.

You Become Easier to Be Around When You Feel Safer Within Yourself - Emotional safety within ourselves can influence the way we experience relationships and interactions with others. When we feel more grounded internally, conversations often become calmer, more natural, and less emotionally exhausting.

This can reduce overthinking, defensiveness, and the pressure to constantly seek reassurance or validation. Feeling safer within yourself often creates greater ease, steadiness, and authenticity in how you connect with others.

We’ve shared a thoughtful reflection on this in our latest blog. You can read it anytime on our website.

The Quiet Confidence of No Longer Needing to Rush Your Life - Many people experience pressure to constantly move faster, achieve more quickly, or have everything figured out immediately. Over time, this urgency can become emotionally exhausting.

Allowing yourself to move at a more sustainable pace can create greater clarity, emotional steadiness, and self-trust. Meaningful growth often develops gradually, and slowing down does not mean you are falling behind.

We’ve shared a thoughtful reflection on this in our latest blog. You can read it anytime on our website.

You Stop Chasing Every Thought That Enters Your Mind: The mind naturally produces many thoughts throughout the day, especially during periods of stress, uncertainty, or overwhelm. However, not every thought requires analysis or immediate attention.

Learning to observe thoughts without reacting to each one can help reduce mental exhaustion and overthinking.
Emotional wellbeing often improves when we become more intentional about where we place our attention and energy.

We’ve shared a thoughtful reflection on this in our latest blog. You can read it anytime on our website.

You Feel More Like Yourself When You Stop Overthinking Every Interaction -
It’s common to replay conversations and reflect on how we communicated. However, constant overthinking can create unnecessary mental pressure and self-doubt.

Allowing interactions to end without repeated analysis can help reduce stress and support more natural communication. When you trust how you show up in the moment, conversations begin to feel more comfortable and authentic.

We’ve shared a thoughtful reflection on this in our latest blog. You can read it anytime on our website.

You Start Responding Differently Without Realising It - Personal growth is not always visible in big or dramatic ways. Often, it appears in small, everyday moments - in how you respond to situations that once felt more intense or overwhelming.

You may begin to notice a greater sense of pause, more thoughtful reactions, and less emotional urgency.
These subtle shifts reflect increased self-awareness and emotional steadiness over time.

We’ve shared a thoughtful reflection on this in our latest blog. You can read it anytime on our website.

Many people ignore strange sensations in their legs until the pain becomes severe. But your body often gives warning signs much earlier.
If you experience tingling in legs, burning sensation in legs, or a constant pins and needles sensation, it could be a sign of nerve pain in leg caused by irritation or compression of nerves.
One of the most common reasons behind these symptoms is sciatica nerve pain, where the sciatic nerve gets irritated in the lower back or hip. This can lead to leg numbness causes, tingling in legs, and sometimes even leg weakness causes. Many people also experience a burning sensation in legs that travels down the thigh or calf.
In some cases, nerve compression symptoms can develop due to prolonged sitting, poor posture, disc irritation, or tight muscles. When the nerve is irritated, it can produce sensations like pins and needles sensation, tingling in legs, or sharp nerve pain in leg.
Another possible reason for these symptoms is peripheral neuropathy symptoms, where nerves become sensitive and start sending abnormal signals like burning sensation in legs, numbness, or weakness.
Sometimes people also notice leg swelling causes along with heaviness and discomfort, which may increase pressure around nerves and worsen sciatica symptoms or nerve compression symptoms.
The good news is that many of these problems can improve with proper physiotherapy for nerve pain.

At first glance, it looks like this person is simply strapped to a moving table... but what if I told you this machine is actually creating space inside the spine to help relieve back pain and sciatica?
What you're seeing is Spinal Decompression Therapy, a specialized non-surgical treatment commonly used for people suffering from chronic lower back pain, sciatica, bulging discs, herniated discs, and certain degenerative spinal conditions.
So how does it work?
The motorized table applies a gentle, controlled pulling force to the lumbar spine (lower back). This creates a process called **decompression**, where the vertebrae are slightly separated, reducing pressure on the spinal discs and nearby nerves.
Why is this important?
🦴 Reduces Disc Pressure
Spinal discs act as shock absorbers between your vertebrae. When a disc bulges or herniates, it can press on nearby nerves and cause pain, numbness, or tingling down the leg. Decompression may help reduce this pressure.
💧 Improves Nutrient Exchange
Unlike many tissues in the body, spinal discs have a very limited blood supply. The gentle stretching and relaxation cycles help encourage the movement of water, oxygen, and nutrients into the discs, supporting their health and recovery.
While spinal decompression can be beneficial for the right patient, it isn't a one-size-fits-all solution. A proper assessment is always important to determine the root cause of your pain.

Frozen Shoulder (Adhesive Capsulitis) is more than just shoulder pain or muscle tightness.
Many people believe it develops from overuse, but the real problem often occurs inside the shoulder joint capsule.
As inflammation builds, the capsule gradually thickens and stiffens, leading to shoulder stiffness, limited shoulder mobility, and difficulty performing simple daily activities like reaching overhead, dressing, or sleeping comfortably.
What makes frozen shoulder unique is its strong association with diabetes, thyroid disorders, and hormonal changes. These underlying conditions can influence the tissues surrounding the joint and increase the risk of developing adhesive capsulitis.
The good news? Early clinical assessment and the right physiotherapy approach can help manage pain, improve shoulder mobility, restore movement, and support shoulder rehabilitation.
Treatment is most effective when tailored to the stage of the condition rather than using the same exercises for everyone.
If your shoulder movement is gradually decreasing, don't ignore the warning signs. Understanding the cause is the first step toward recovery.

A controlled traction technique helps decompress the joint surfaces, allowing them to move more freely with less restriction.

When joints become stiff, your body starts compensating during walking, squatting, climbing stairs, and even simple daily activities. Over time, these movement compensations can contribute to discomfort, reduced mobility, and unnecessary strain on surrounding muscles.

Muscles need stretching.
Joints need mobilization.
The right combination can help you move better, feel lighter, and reduce that constant feeling of heaviness or stiffness.
